title: How Observability and Monitoring Come Together
subtitle: Use aggregates to notice, events to investigate
summary: Monitoring remains useful in an observable system. Compact measurements can track expected conditions, trends, and service health without retaining every contributing detail. Their limitation appears when an investigation asks a question that the aggregation did not preserve. Events and traces provide the finer context needed to examine a specific request or unexpected cohort. The chapter brings these approaches together through their purposes rather than treating one data type as a universal replacement for another. Teams should understand which information a summary discards and preserve a route from a concerning aggregate to relevant examples. This combination supports efficient detection while reducing the guesswork involved in explaining partial failures and unfamiliar behavior.

concepts.title: Metrics trade detail for efficiency
concepts.body: A metric compresses observations into a measurement with a chosen set of labels and an interval. Reusing those combinations can make collection and querying economical. That efficiency comes from deciding what to retain; if an omitted attribute later matters, the aggregate cannot reconstruct the individual requests that contributed to it.
concepts.example: A fleet error counter reveals a rise but omits the failing customers.

concepts.title: Events retain the investigation unit
concepts.body: An event keeps attributes together at the request or operation level. It can support new groupings when an unexpected question appears, provided the relevant fields were recorded. This costs more than keeping only a total, but preserves a path to discovering whether a broad symptom comes from one cohort or many unrelated situations.
concepts.example: Compare errors by build and tenant using the original request records.

concepts.title: Different signals serve different questions
concepts.body: Monitoring can answer whether a known condition needs attention, while exploration asks what is happening inside the affected population. Both can coexist around the same service. Choosing a signal should begin with its job: a capacity trend, an actionable reliability alert, and a specific customer investigation need different levels of detail.
concepts.example: Use a utilization trend for capacity planning and traces to explain one slow checkout.

concepts.title: Connect summaries to retained context
concepts.body: An alert or graph is a stronger starting point when the responder can inspect relevant events with its time range and scope preserved. Without that connection, responders may search unrelated logs or trace samples and infer a relationship from timing alone. The handoff should retain enough context to keep the investigation focused on the actual symptom.
concepts.example: An error-rate graph opens the corresponding failing endpoint requests.

misconceptions.correction: Metrics remain efficient for known measurements and trends; detailed exploration has different requirements.

misconceptions.claim: A more detailed graph can recover dimensions discarded during aggregation.
misconceptions.correction: Presentation cannot restore request attributes that the stored summary never retained.

scenario.title: The aggregate has no tenant field
scenario.context: An error graph spikes, but its labels contain only service and status.

options.label: Investigate matching request events
options.benefit: Can identify which tenants and builds contribute to the spike.
options.cost: Requires a retained event source and aligned time range.
options.consequence: The team can estimate impact and locate the affected customer population.

options.label: Add tenant labels to the metric for future traffic
options.benefit: May support a specific recurring tenant-level measurement.
options.cost: Cannot recover past context and may greatly expand time-series cardinality.
options.consequence: Future metrics change, but the current incident still requires another evidence source.

scenario.debrief: Use the retained event evidence for this incident and choose future metric labels for their intended measurement.

quiz.question: A metric omits tenant identity. Can its graph later show the exact failing tenants?
options: No; it needs another data source retaining that context
Yes, by reducing the graph interval
Yes, by changing the aggregate from average to maximum
quiz.explanation: The stored information limits the questions; a display cannot recreate omitted attributes.

quiz.question: Which pairing fits the chapter?
options: Metrics for both detection and exact reconstruction of omitted request details
Metrics for known signals, events for exploratory diagnosis
Events for finding known failures, metrics for arbitrary new dimensions
quiz.explanation: The approaches complement each other when their respective detail and cost are understood.

quiz.question: An alert opens a trace viewer with no filters. What would improve the handoff?
options: Showing the newest trace regardless of scope
Opening a week of all service traces to provide maximum context
Preserving the affected time range and request population
quiz.explanation: The responder needs examples relevant to the signal, not merely access to another tool.
